title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: DENISE NAPPIER
affiliation: PRINCIPLE FIDUCIARY, STATE TREASURER, CONNECTICUT RETIREMENT PLAN AND TRUST FUND
speaker: Investor
text:
Chairman Tillerson, members of the Board of Directors and my fellow shareholders, my name is Denise Nappier, Treasurer of the State of Connecticut and Principle Fiduciary of the $25 billion Connecticut Retirement Plan and Trust Fund. We hold over 3.8 million shares of  ExxonMobil stock, with a current value in excess of $300 million. So it represents our largest single investment.   

I stand here today to move resolution number five, filed by Ram Trust Services to request the Board separate the positions of Chairman and CEO. Now although we rarely favor one all-powerful CEO and Chair, we recognize that some companies attempt to balance power by designating a lead director to ensure some independent Board oversight.   

Our company,  ExxonMobil, does not even have a lead independent director. In fact, our company's corporate governance guidelines state that, and I quote, "The Board does not believe it is useful or appropriate to designate a lead non-employee director."   

Well perhaps this is a way for  ExxonMobil to avoid any inconvenient truths. In considering this lack of independent leadership on the Board, it is no wonder there's no process for shareholders to meet with members of the Board of Directors on issues critical to the long-term value of our shares.   

The Connecticut Pension Fund and other major shareholders have requested a meeting with Michael Boskin, Chair of our Public Issues Committee and we have been turned down five times. Now our purpose for the meeting is quite simple. To have constructive dialogue with Professor Boskin on climate change, and the implication for sustaining our company's stellar performance out into the future.   

Now climate change may be about our planet's future, but it's also about the financial implication to company's such as  ExxonMobil. And the impact on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, including Connecticut's active workers and retirees, whose pension fund assets are committed to my care.   

As the result, we have every right to know what the company is doing, and how it will protect their -- our company's bottom line. This issue is not going away and neither are we. I believe that we as shareholders, and I'm talking about shareholders representing in excess of $1 trillion, on this issue of open communication.   

I think that we agree that  ExxonMobil needs to raise the bar on its corporate governance practices. We do have a common ground with our company. We all are interested in the bottom line. And I believe that if we can [marshal] our resources, we will be able to preserve our future economy. Thank you very much, and with that in mind, I hope this meeting begins a new day of  ExxonMobil, one of openness and long-term vision.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: JONATHAN DILL
speaker: Investor
text:
Good morning. I write today on behalf of literally thousands of long-term  ExxonMobil shareholders who wish to benefit far more directly than you are permitting us to do so now, from the extraordinary successes of our company. We wish to remain long-term investors in our company, while sharing equitably in the rewards of our success without the need to sell some of our investment.   

As long-term shareholders, we benefit from your policy of raising the base dividend rate each year. However, we also wish to benefit directly and meaningful from periods of exceptionally large free cash flows such as our company has realized in the past several years.   

We as shareholders with no interest in selling our stock have not, do not and will not benefit meaningfully, directly or equitably from the massive share repurchases made by the Board. Your policy of refusing to distribute a greater percentage of our company's free cash flow in the form of special or extra dividends, denies us any meaningful or bankable benefits from these extraordinary successes.   

Mr. Chairman and members of the Board, we are different than you are. We cannot vote ourselves nor have our friends on the Compensation Committee vote for us new shares of stock each year. We do not have the ability to sell $6 million worth of shares in the secure knowledge that our friends on the Compensation Committee will replace these shares next year.   

The  ExxonMobil shares we have are all the shares we are ever likely to have. And if we sell our shares, our future level of investment and our future income will be irredeemably reduced. Also Mr. Chairman, unlike you, we do believe that special dividends directly and importantly benefit long-term shareholders. Your argumentation in favor of share repurchases at the expense of special dividends is simply wrong.   

Special dividends have two very important benefits to the long-term investors. One, special dividends allow us to share meaningfully in the profits of our company by using those special dividends to meet our other financial obligations. This is an extraordinarily important benefit for all long-term investors that cannot be realized through a program of share repurchases, as selling our shares would only reduce our level of future income.   

You can think of the special dividend as our equivalent to your annual bonus. When our company earns it, we should get some of it. Two, the policy of declaring special dividends as situations warrant would increase the share price of  ExxonMobil stock and in a manner similar to the Board's policy of very heavy share repurchasing.   

When prospects for  ExxonMobil are good, people will bid up the price of stock because they know there is a prospect that the Board might declare a special dividend. Of course as we all know, events in Iraq, Iran, Venezuela and Nigeria and Russia and elsewhere, over which the Board has no control, have far more impact on our share price, for better or worse, than the Board's share repurchase program will ever have.   

However a policy of paying periodic special dividends as situations warrant would directly benefit every shareholder, regardless of events in Nigeria or elsewhere, while at the same time having a beneficial effect on the share price, probably at least as powerful as the Board's massive share buyback program. Our dividend pay-out ratio has declined steadily over the past years, while the growth in share repurchases has been exponential. In just the last four years --.

That the time is now for you to accept this, particularly because much of the issue came about with regard to executive compensation plans with Exxon itself. Thank you, very much.

text:
Thank you. When the history of this time is written it will be observed that the relationship between a corporation and their principal officers has changed fundamentally. The traditional role was that a Chief Executive Officer was a professional who was very well paid for being a professional.   

And the pattern which has emerged in the last several years has been that the CEO has become a partner of the shareholders. In this guise, Exxon has a leadership responsibility. As I mentioned to you at the last Annual Meeting, Mr. Tillerson, your predecessor's pay, Mr. Raymond, was 16 times larger than that of Mr. Rawl. And as I remarked at that time, if you can keep this tradition going, you might actually be a rich man.   

But aside from that, the ratio between what a CEO is paid and others are paid has also gone way up. So at a time of historic change, a bylaw provision would be inappropriate unless we were talking about something where there was change of this magnitude. I have to recount to you a personal experience, the first American employee to be paid $1 billion in the course of his life was the CEO of Coca Cola.   

I've been told by two personal friends, who were Directors of Coca Cola, that at no time was that arrangement ratified by the Board. Now there are times, Mr. Chairman, when candor gets lost in politeness. It is sometimes difficult for even the most outspoken people to be confrontational.   

The purpose of this bylaw us to provide some kind of protection for Directors by saying that there must be an explicit vote, an explicit vote by two thirds of the Independent Directors specifically ratifying the arrangement. If we are going to change history, if the new model of CEO as a substantial owner of the company, as partner, is going to become part of American corporate practice, then it is important that this be memorialized by formal action of the Board. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

My name is Julie Goodridge. I am the President of NorthStar Asset Management and the beneficial owner of 4,400 shares of  ExxonMobil. I'm here to ask for your support on resolution number nine, a request for an Executive Compensation Report that we also presented last year.   

25 years ago the average CEO compensation package was 42 times higher than the average worker's pay, now the average CEO makes 411 times more than the average worker. Our CEO, who earns a lot less than our former CEO, still makes 759 times what the average worker makes in this country. Last year our company gave our former CEO, Lee Raymond, a lump sum retirement benefit of $98 million at a time when the company's employee pension plan had an $11.2 billion funding deficit.   

Due in part to our former CEO's exorbitant compensation, executive compensation in general is under greater scrutiny by the Securities and Exchange Commission, by Congress, by the media and by shareholders. In fact, Mr. Raymond's pay package was held as a deplorable example by Representative Barney Frank of Massachusetts, when the House still requiring public companies to give shareholders an annual nonbinding vote on executive compensation, was passed by the House of Representatives.   

Senator Obama introduced a Companion Bill in the Senate. New SEC rules aim to uncover the full extent of executive compensation. Exxon's Proxy Statement reports, Mr. Tillerson in his first year as our CEO took home just over $13 million. However if we calculate Mr. Tillerson's compensation using new SEC rules, we find that Mr. Tillerson's actual compensation is over $22 million.   

We believe the historically high executive compensation level of our company diminishes shareholder value. We are asking our company to examine the significant gap between the lowest paid worker and the highest paid worker, because we believe it is fiscally irresponsible for a company to put so much of its resources in one individual. Our resolution asks shareholders to join us in questioning, why it takes our lowest paid employee a full year to earn what Mr. Tillerson earns for an hour on the job?   

We believe that reinvesting  ExxonMobil's history making profits of 2006 in all of  ExxonMobil's employees, from the line workers to Administrative Assistants to Management, will increase shareholder value by strengthening employee morale and protecting us from declining value when times are less favorable. A fresh look at our executive compensation will show that in times of profit we plan for our company's future. Thank you.

This resolution focuses on  ExxonMobil's impact in local communities. You will hear a great deal about the company's impact on the global environment, but as the name implies, the Foreign and Domestic Missionary Society is concerned about poor people, people who are voiceless, in the communities where  ExxonMobil operates.   

Although Exxon prides itself on its environmental performance and has much, much to be commended for, no spills, its safety record is truly exceptional and it publishes one of the best Corporate Citizenship Reports among the corporations. However, what is sorely lacking from this report is information about the impact of Exxon's operations in local communities.   

The resolution cites -- one of the reasons for -- several of the reasons for our concern, one of which was the 2005 settlement with EPA of $570 million in pollution control technology to be installed in Exxon's seven US refineries. A more recent report has found that three of Exxon's refineries rank among the top ten sources of carcinogenic air emissions in the United States, this is 2004 data. The Baytown, Texas refinery was number two, Baton Rouge number six, Chalmette, Louisiana number nine.   

The third reason for our concern is the growing environmental liabilities reported by the company for years 2002 to 2005. We note that reserves in 2003 or supported in 2003 stood at 468 million, expenditures 215 million, new accruals 275 million. New accruals have grown every year for 2002, '03 and '04, in 2005 they dropped a bit, but reserves have increased substantially as have expenditures.   

Unfortunately from the information published we do not know exactly why. We do not know if this is legacy pollution such as we have in Brooklyn, New York, for which the company is being sued by the New York State Attorney General. We do not know if this is from ongoing operations, and we certainly, as community residents, do not know what the immediate impacts are on health and safety in our communities.   

Therefore, we ask Exxon to join with the growing best practices of the corporate community, as endorsed by the  International Finance Corporation in their guidance on stakeholder engagement, A Good Practice Handbook, to utilize the facility's reporting tools developed by (inaudible) and to begin to have good ongoing relationships in the communities where you operate. Mr. Chairman, members of the Board, shareholders, my name is Eric Lalanne, I'm here on behalf of my father, [Mateo], a single shareholder who has sponsored proposal number 16. Concerns about greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide or CO2 are rising fast.   

Yet, at the service point where millions of daily transactions take place, there is no mention of CO2 emissions, be it on the bill, the receipts or any other appropriate means of disclosure. As a result, only a small minority realizes that each gallon of gasoline contains five pounds of carbon that generates, while burning, almost 20 pounds of CO2. In other words, 400 pounds of CO2 are sent up in the sky for every 20 gallon tank that is emptied.   

Since energy has already been spent to find, extract, transport and refine these 20 gallons to the service station, much CO2 has already been emitted bringing the total closer to 500 pounds. [Fairly] significant changes, this trend will be going up due to increased reliance on oil sands and difficulties associated with pipeline delivery for ethanol laced gasoline. Unless this corporation figures this out and informs customers, how could they ever have realistic appreciation of the situation?   

All the buzz about one carbon footprint and how to offset it, it is clear indication that the quantitative data describing greenhouse gases generated by fuel consumption, might soon be regarded as basic information that customers are entitled to each time they buy fuel. It would be timely for  ExxonMobil to take the leadership in developing, and in systematically applying consumer-friendly information about CO2 emissions, enabling the ultimate decision maker in the marketplace to eventually make better decisions.   

Either  ExxonMobil takes the leadership in this matter, or there is a great risk that it will be forced by numerous governments to comply to many different less consistent and less practical information disclosure requirements, because concerns about CO2 emissions will not fade away. Shareholders would benefit from  ExxonMobil's decisiveness, or they may suffer prejudice if this opportunity is missed.   

Every time consumers buy gasoline or diesel fuel, making sure that they are given a reasonable estimate of how much CO2 emissions are related to their consumption is not a trivial task. It would not be beyond  ExxonMobil's expertise and willingness to share this information with the general public.   

This proposal gives the Board latitude to implement gradually over time and space, therefore it is proposed that the shareholders adopt the following resolution, that  ExxonMobil Corporation inform its customers about the carbon dioxide CO2 emissions generated by the gasoline and diesel fuel that they buy.   

The quantitative information would be provided at the pump, and based on average well-to-wheel figures, i.e. encompassing all faces from extraction up and including consumption. In other words, it is time for this company to take on this tough energy challenge. Thank you.

[ CalPERS] holds 30 million shares of  ExxonMobil valued at $2.5 billion and  CalSTRS holds 21 million shares of  ExxonMobil common stock with a market value of $1.7 billion.   

As Controller, on behalf of Chuck Valdez, our Investment Committee Chair and the Board of CalPERS, we wanted to make very clear our strong concern about the failure of communication between the members of the Board of Directors and your share owners. We are in this together, we want to work together to make sure that we have the strongest and best fiscal practices and business practices, so that  ExxonMobil can continue to be a global leader. We saw a very strong business plan. We wanted to focus on your vision and your statement and your focus.   

The display you had clearly states that you want to work on officially providing valuable products that improve quality of life, progress through technology, supporting CO2 mitigation. We support all of those practices, however we don't think that we're working strongly and aggressively and smartly enough on these types of issues.   

We think they have extraordinary impact,  CalPERS and  CalSTRS has been a leader in terms of assessment of climate risk and its return on rates to the shareholder, Exxon's [boastful] approach on renewable energy, its resistant to a strong national climate policy, its obstruction on climate science, is not befitting of  ExxonMobil's international leadership and stature. We want to work with you to enhance shareholder value and build the best business practices.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: KENNETH J. DUKE
affiliation: SHAREHOLDER, BATON ROUGE REFINERY & CHEMICAL SITE
speaker: Investor
text:
Mr. Tillerson, members of the Board, I am [Kenneth J. Duke]. I'm the USW Safety Officer at the Baton Rouge Refinery and Chemical site.  ExxonMobil has a primary stated objective to bring the stockholders a long-term return, this is providing operational excellence.   

ExxonMobil high priority is said to be leadership in safety, health and environment, but recently  ExxonMobil has made tremendous profits, and the largest in history, and we're sitting on piles of money. As many consumers I would like to see $2 a gallon gas, but I know that's not possible. As a shareholder I would like to see huge dividends and I hope that this would be possible in the future.   

But if these can't be done, I would like to see that money placed back into our business. This only makes good business sense. Over the past decade,  ExxonMobil has made drastic cuts in manpower and maintenance. It is my opinion that this safety has been harmed by such cost cutting, production pressures and failure to invest in maintenance and infrastructure. When I raise such items locally, we we're told that OIMS, Operation Integrity Operation Management System would prevent accidents from happening.   

However, having good systems in place does not help if they're not used properly or pushed to the limits. There is too much emphasis being placed on personnel safety and not on enough on process safety. We're risk assessing too often.   

We're running operations on the ragged edge of safety. Our risk assessing operations is as if we were driving a car on four bald tires, we're getting along now but one of these days we're going to have a blowout. Because we have been so efficient and so safe in the past, doesn't necessarily mean that we will be so in the future.   

I don't want to see an explosion like happened at Texas City happen at our site in Baton Rouge. It's common sense to use some of our recent record profits of our corporation to improve manpower, training and most of all preventative maintenance and mechanical integrity. I ask the Board members to please consider investing in modernizing and expanding our refining capacity in our existing refineries. Thank you.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: ANDREW LOGAN
affiliation: SHAREHOLDER, INVESTOR NETWORK ON CLIMATE RISK
speaker: Investor
text:
Thank you. I'm Andrew Logan with the Investor Network on Climate Risk and my question is really simple. Why has our company seemingly put so much effort into making itself into public enemy number one on climate change? How have we gotten to this point, where an otherwise great company who has acquired such a dismal reputation, and has become more known more for its funding of climate skeptics than for its technological leadership, which is quite profound?   

It just seemed irrational to me, you're an energy company, your job is to deliver returns to shareholders which you're quite good at, your job is not to be public philosophers on science, though I did enjoy your lecture last year in this meeting on the philosophical impossibility of scientific consensus. Your job is clearly not to do things that harm the company's reputation while bringing no obvious benefits.   

I guess perhaps you could claim that you've benefited shareholders by delaying the day of reckoning for  ExxonMobil on climate change, but I don't see that. It might have been true if you were a coal mining company with limited strategic options, but you're a company with a massive and impressive R&D expertise and huge reserves of natural gas.   

You can turn climate change into an opportunity if you want to, but instead you continue to fund groups like the Heartland Institute that question the science of climate change, and all you can really manage to say on the issue is that the risk from rising greenhouse gas emissions could prove to be significant. Well I could be nominated to the Exxon Board, but I'm not betting on it.   

When you compare that to what some of your peers have said, the head of  ConocoPhillips a few weeks ago said that, "The science on climate change is quite compelling, human activity including the burning of fossil fuel is contributing to climate change. Now is the time for a national mandated framework to deal with climate change. If we wait," he said, "even a few years, it won't be mitigation it'll be adaptation." And this is a clear statement, and this is a company that certainly understands the urgency of climate change.   

And you complain that your position on climate change is misunderstood, but with legalistic statements like the one I quoted, it just seems like you almost want to be misunderstood. So my question really is, why? Why do you allow things to get so out of hand? You sacrifice the company's reputation by taking a position that, to me at least, seems to benefit no one, not the company, not shareholders and certainly not the planet as well. So, thank you.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
Thank you. Let me assure you we never set out for the company to be public enemy number one. As you and I talked last year, I said that there is much we know and can agree on around the climate change issue, and there's much that we just don't believe we do know. And so, there are some areas that we're probably not going to agree on. The position that you described of others is not that different from our position on climate change.   

I think the difference may be around the certainty with which we view some of the predictions, and we're a company that is very comfortable and adept at dealing with a lot of uncertainty. We've been doing that for 125 years. And we deal with that through technology, we deal with it through science, and we deal with it through our positioning in considering the current events in the context of future events and the role that we play.   

So again our position, I don't think, is different than what you describe. What I find perplexing is, why people feel so threatened because we want to have a discussion about it? And we want to have a debate about the things we know and understand, the things we know about that we don't understand very well, and the things that we don't even know about around this very complex issue of climate science.   

So that is going to continue to be our position, we're going to continue to support scientific investigation and discovery around this very crucial issue that affects all of us and our children and our grandchildren. And we're going to continue to support steps that we think can be taken today that will make meaningful difference today, energy efficiency, using the energy more wisely.   

We do not oppose the development of alternative fuels, the fact that we choose not to invest in them does not mean that we are opposed to those. In fact, we are the largest user of ethanol and gasoline today. We used over 10% of the available ethanol in the United States in our blended fuels last year. We will be the largest user again this year.   

So we do not stand in the way of alternatives, we do think there needs to be careful and powerful policy around the framework in which you support the development of alternatives, because we believe that competitive market forces lead to the greatest powers of ingenuity, entrepreneurialship and creativity coming to barrel the problem. So when you put in interfering factors with the policy, you actually interfere with the creativity of the marketplace to deliver a better solution, a more lasting solution.   

So I think we may have a lot of differences of views around how should we go about this, but we don't have a difference of view that it's an important issue, it's a serious issue. There are some things we know, there are some things we don't know and we think it's vital that we understand this issue better so that we can make wiser decisions. Because these are life changing decisions for our children and our grandchildren and we think you ought to be careful about that.   

Now why people don't want to have a discussion about the things we don't know and don't understand, I can't do anything about those people. All I can do is continue to say, "Well look we've been studying this a long time, we've got a lot of smart scientists working on it, and this is what we think we know and what we don't know." And we listen to everybody and we participate in the IPCC Report. Some of our people help write that report. We participate in peer review of reports.   

So we're very engaged on the issue and look at everything, and we listen to everything. But I'm not going to put a banner up, and I'm not going to adopt a slogan. If that's what you say it takes to make me not be public enemy number one, I'm not going there because that's just not honest.   

Next question or comment? The gentlemen in the back? Yes. We'll try to get around to everybody.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: SAMIR LUTHER
speaker: Investor
text:
Good morning, and thank you very much. My name is Samir Luther and I'm here with the Human Rights Campaign in support of item number 13 to amend  ExxonMobil's Equal Employment Opportunity Policy. Since 1995 the Human Rights Campaign has tracked Fortune ranked companies and their treatment of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender employees. And since 1999 we have asked you, the Directors of the combined Exxon and Mobil Corporation, to reinstate the fair policies that Mobil Corporation once had.   

Each year you have claimed that you don't discriminate based on sexual orientation, and that you don't need to formalize this in your Equal Employment Opportunity Policy. And once again the Board recommends a vote against this proposal, as outlined on page 57 and 58 of the Proxy Statement. I point you though to the top 50 Fortune ranked companies.   

All of them, with the exception of this company, have added sexual orientation to their Equal Employment Opportunity Policy. In fact, each of the US based companies represented by members of this Board, including Haliburton, Verizon and the  American Electric Power Company have taken this step.   

You proudly invest in the future scientists And Mathematicians of America, your future workforce, but you turn your back on the thousands of gay scientists and mathematicians who have better options and benefits at every single large competitor of this company, including  Chevron, BP and Shell.   

Your rationale as outlined in this Proxy Statement does not change the fact that  ExxonMobil is the only Fortune 50 company that has not taken this step. Your employees and your shareholders deserve more. I urge  ExxonMobil shareholders to vote for this resolution, item number 13. Thank you.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: SHAWNEE HOOVER
speaker: Investor
text:
Thank you very much, Mr. Tillerson, Board of Directors, shareholders. My name is Shawnee Hoover, I am the Campaign Director with Exxpose Exxon, I'm not sure you quite want to hear from me today, but I hope so. In regards to actually what you just said, I find it very interesting. In January in DAVOS, Mr. Tillerson, you said it is not useful to debate the issue any longer. And we really supported that and we were actually looking for the company to support it as well.   

Last year Exxon gave $11 million to combat malaria, and educate girls and women in Africa, but what was in the news? It was the funding of think tanks and organizations that deny the science which is unequivocal, we've heard it, we've heard it before, enter governmental panel on climate change, 2,500 scientists. Shell has actually said, "Who are we to contradict the scientists of the IPCC?"   

So we do urge the company to leave the science on climate to the scientists, and deal with the conclusions from there. There are hundreds of  ExxonMobil shareholders involved with the Exxpose Exxon Campaign, hundreds of them.   

Each one of the people standing here represent over 30 shareholders each who contacted us after we sent a small email educating people about the resolutions that were on Exxon's agenda this year to just a fraction of our list, 80,000 people. We got 300, almost 350 responses from shareholders giving their proxy and giving other information.   

So I would like to conclude by saying that there are hundreds of thousands of people, 500,000 people who have joined on with the campaign, that are very concerned about Exxon's contradiction of the science, its funding of these front groups. And just real quick to end, I just want to say when you talk about debate, the Heartland Institute and policy, in 2007 State Legislative Guidebook claims that "warming is likely to be very modest relative to natural variations.   

Benefits are likely to outweigh costs and taking action now in the name of fighting global warming is unnecessary." That is really not the kind of debate, I think, that you're talking about. There's things we know, there's things we don't know, this is not the type of debate that Exxon really should be funding. So we urge you please to stop funding these groups. Thanks.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
Thank you. Well in some sense you're accurate in my statement at DAVOS where I said it's not useful to debate this issue, and I was talking about the science of it. And that's because most people that want to debate the science issue are not competent to debate it. And so it's not, as I said I think last year, there's probably a lot of areas around the science where you and I are just not going to agree, okay? But that doesn't mean you stop the scientific investigation, better understanding, collecting more data. This is a really complex problem.   

I know people like to boil it down to something very simple, very simple. The polar ice caps are melting, the planet's seven tenths of a degree centigrade warmer, we're using more fossil fuels, that's all you need to know, it's really that simple of an equation. It's really not that simple of an equation, and all of the scientists that are part of the IPCC know it's not that simple of an equation.   

And the groups that we support at MIT, at Battelle Research, at Yale University, at Stanford University, at the University of Texas, a broad range of various academic and scientific institutions. We're supporting them because we want their help to understand this better. And I think these are some of the very best minds working on this issue, and we do talk to them and meet with them on a regular basis to say, "Help us understand this."   

Some of the scientists you refer to in the IPCC community of scientists are our scientists. We're part of that. So we're in that debate, we're in that discussion and debate is good, debate is healthy. The issue is serious. Now we can have another kind of debate then around what are we going to do about?   

We agree we need to be taking some steps. But when you don't really have a very, very clear, crystal clear understanding and predictive capability of what the steps you may take will produce in the way of an outcome, you are really betting the farm. You're really betting the farm when you start putting in place broad reaching policies that are going to affect economic conditions, poverty for the rest of the world and a number of other social issues which are important to be addressed.   

And when we don't put it in that context, then I think we deny, those who won't put it in that context deny, the importance of this issue. So we're going to continue to try to have very constructive conversations around this to arrive at good long-term policy decisions. And we welcome the engagement, and we've had engagement with a number of groups, we're going to continue that. As I said, if that makes us not Shell, well based on my results I'm kind of glad I'm not Shell.   

The lady down in front here.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting

text:
Thank you, Mr. Tillerson. My name is John Wilson, I'm with Christian Brothers Investment Services, we are owners of 658,000 shares of  ExxonMobil. We are also one of the co-filers of resolution number 15 asking the company to adopt reduction targets for carbon emissions.   

We hope that the shareholders present will support that resolution. But more important than one company's efforts to reduce its carbon emissions from products as well as operations, are national and international goals for doing the same thing through the mechanism of public policy.   

And as you know, many Bills are now presently being considered in Congress regarding climate change, some of which go by the name of Carbon Taxes, others by Cap and Trade Systems. All of which have really the same goal which is to reduce the amount of carbon that we are emitting into the atmosphere and to mitigate the worst effects of climate change.   

Now some of the representatives of  ExxonMobil have indicated that there might be some interest in supporting some of these pieces of legislation. But at the same time, as we look at your Annual Report, we see that your projections for the energy future over the next 20 to 25 years says that, as energy demand rises globally, the mix of energy sources will remain the same with liquids being about 80%.   

So this seems to raise some confusion about what your expectations are because that kind of future, which is the status quo, saying the future is the same as the present will lead to environmental tragedy, which has been well documented elsewhere and discussed here today.   

So I guess my question for you, if you could provide some clarity about that, do you support legislation on climate? Under what circumstances would you support constraint on carbon emissions? And then, what do you hope that those pieces of legislation will achieve long term, if not a change in the status quo? Thank you.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
Well I hope that you had the opportunity to visit one of the displays in the foyer outside where we're doing the technology displays. There's a display devoted to greenhouse gas emissions, it has some measures of our own in terms of how we're doing over the last few years, and there are some points there about our future.   

As I've indicated, what we are doing around our own operations is, first trying to become more energy efficient so that we can carry out the same level of activities, consuming less energy, which reduces our overall greenhouse gas emissions.   

We have some very substantive investment programs under way to eliminate flaring of gas, which is a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions, largely in Africa where, because of the remoteness of those operations, there is no outlet for the gas. So most of this involves capturing the gas and reinjecting it back into the ground where hopefully in the future it'll have some economic value to the country.   

The third area is technology and when you talk about our energy outlook, which is 60% liquids, 20% coal, so it's 80% fossil fuels, is the outlook. And that's simply based on a realistic look at what is likely to be able to be provided in the way of other options on a global scale that's necessary to change that relative mix.   

And that's taking into consideration things like double-digit growth in solar and wind energy, that's in that outlook. Now there's nothing else out there growing double-digit rates, that I know of, over a long period of time, but we have incorporated double-digit growth rates. But even with double-digit growth rates, as I'm sure you know, by the time you get 25 years out, they still only account for 1% or 2% of total energy supply because you start from such a very small base.   

And that's one of the challenges of just the enormous scale of the energy supply situation to support economic activity the world over and that's why we don't think the mix is going to change substantially over the next 25 years. If you look beyond that, obviously it's hard enough to look out 25 years, but if you go further some of these technologies that we all hope for in the way of breakthroughs, whether it's in biofuels or nuclear energy coming back on the table, over time we hope will have a significant impact.   

So, how do I reconcile my position? It's back to technology because it's going to be developing ways to use the energy that we have, predominantly fossil fuels, in ways that limit, minimize the greenhouse gas emissions. And that's where a lot of our technology investment today is being made because it's built on that belief the world, like it or not, is going to have to continue to consume largely and live off of fossil fuel. So we've got to learn how to use them differently.   

Now it's fine if people want to work on ways to replace them, and we don't feel threatened by that at all, but we're not in that business. we're in the business of producing oil and natural gas, so we want to devote our time and attention to technologies that change the way we use those fuels, in a way that allows us to meet some of the objectives of lower emissions.   

So that is why our partnerships, and I'm glad someone mentioned Toyota being the leading automotive company, because Toyota is our automotive partner.  Caterpillar for heavy industrial engines define ways to bring more fuel efficiencies to those two forms of transportation and industrial use that will lower the overall emissions from those activities.   

As all of you know, our support creation of the Global Climate Energy Project at Stanford, which is trying to leap out 50 years to 60 years out, leap over the periods we [now] and then and say what could, what might be possible 50 60 years from now? Because you've got to start working on it today.   

So, there's no reconciliation difficulty with our statements and our objectives and our technology investments. We are going to continue to invest in, near terms and intermediate terms, ways to allow consumers to use fossil fuels that are less damaging to the environment.   

Now, why do we have confidence in that? Because if I look backwards to the 1970s, if you take the same automobile in 1970 and put that on the road today, that automobile is emitting 97% fewer pollutants than it was in 1970. And that's been through a whole host of technology and fuels advancements, clean fuels, working with engine manufacturers for the way fuels are burned, catalytic converters, weight, I mean there are just a whole host of technologies that are going to have to come to bear on this question.   

We're going to try to participate in areas where we have some expertise, which is fuels, lubricants, the way those are used and the way they burn. That's why we have confidence that in the future there can be significant progress made in how we use fossil fuels. And somewhere out there, probably not in my lifetime probably not in yours, there will be something other than fossil fuels.   

But it's on a scale that's needed to support the world economic growth and on a scale that's needed to support the eradication of poverty, provide fresh drinking water to the almost 2 billion people that don't have it, electricity to the almost 3 billion people that don't have it, and that has to be done to address so many of our social ills in this world that we live in. You're going to have to use fossil fuels. You can deny that if you like, but that's the fact. So, we're going to work on the things that we know how to do.   

The gentlemen in the blue shirt.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: KIRK MILLER
speaker: Investor
text:
Chairman Tillerson, members of the Board of Directors, fellow shareholders, my name is Kirk Miller and I am an  ExxonMobil shareholder and also a Stanford alumnus. I'm here today to speak in support of shareholder resolution number 15. I'd first like to say that I represent a group of concerned Stanford alumni, and we appreciate the goals of the Global Climate & Energy Program, GCEP, that is being funded at Stanford University. We appreciate the donation to Stanford from all four of the GCEP funders including Exxon.   

However, many Stanford alumni are very unhappy with Exxon's actions on funding junk science and inaction on a near-term climate strategy. You just mentioned that the solutions from GCEP are 50 to 60 years away, and I agree, they're long term, they're extremely valuable, the question is what are you doing in the near term?   

Stanford has voted to support [shareholder] number 15 asking for substantive targets based on current technologies. This is important for the Board to recognize. The very institution that is the centerpiece of Exxon's Climate Change strategy is voting against you on near-term climate action, and lack of action and funding of junk science.   

All of Exxon's main competitors have set substantive quantitative goals for greenhouse gas reduction. Many have already exceeded the targets. Exxon has refused to set those targets for products and operations. We had a meeting last year with Henry Hubble, we talked about it, we had many areas where we agreed but targets were not set.   

Mr. Tillerson has outlined many areas where Exxon is an industry leader, Exxon understands leadership. The strongest applause that you got today were for comments on your dedication to the difficult challenge of climate change.   

I would like to join you next year in applause for true leadership in solving this very, very difficult challenge. There is no more difficult challenge than climate change. I would ask you to set the challenge to the 82,000 employees, set the bar high, do it now. Take on the world's toughest energy challenge. I appreciate your time.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
Thank you. Well I think we've had a thorough discussion of all the business items now. If any of you have proxy cards, please hand them to the ushers at this time. Those who have already returned their proxy cards need not vote by ballot unless you wish to change your vote. If you wish to change your vote, simply mark the appropriate sections of the ballot.   

The ballots will now be collected and turned over the Inspectors of Election to be counted. If you wish your ballot to be kept secret, the usher will provide you with an envelope. The appointed proxies in attendance today hereby cast all votes which we have been authorized to cast in accordance with instructions indicated on the individual proxy cards. So if you have any proxies to pass along to the ushers, they are making their way up the aisles now.   

Since proxies and ballots have been collected, I now declare the polls closed. While the Inspectors of Election are preparing their preliminary report, I'm happy to open the floor back up for a few more questions about our business. I'll interrupt those discussions when the Inspectors of Election are ready to give their voting report, and then I'll conclude the meeting.   

Just as a transition if I could, let me take one question at least, we've had many that have come across the Internet, but I'll take one question that's come across the Internet. Now the question is, a new refinery hasn't been built in over 30 years while demand has dramatically increased in that time. If you and the other major oil companies don't get together and build another refinery, aren't you in effect controlling the supply of gasoline and so the supply and demand equation?   

Well it's true that a new refinery has not been built in this country for more than 30 years and there are any number of reasons why. Economics most principally because for most of the last 30 years the economics of refining have not been particularly robust. It's in many a years been a single-digit return business and there's not very many people that want to take the risk in a refining business to earn a single-digit return.   

Having said that though, there's been a lot of rationalization in the refining industry over the last 30 years and all of you have heard the numbers of the refineries that have been closed down. That's actually been a very positive thing because it has brought a lot of efficiency to the refining infrastructure in this country.   

The refineries that are running today are much more efficient, they're much more capacity efficient, and they're much more capable of adapting to the evermore demanding environmental requirements from both an operating standpoint to manage emissions from our refineries, waste water discharges, as well as meet the very stringent fuel specifications that the consumers have demanded, or at least their policy makers in Washington perceive the consumers are demanding. So the laws have been put in place to make these very clean fuels.   

So the circuit that's in place today is really quite efficient and effective, and it has grown in its capacity, as I mentioned in my remarks, our own capacity has grown 50% more than industry's capacity over the last decade. And our capacity on our existing sites has grown in lock step with rising gasoline and fuels demands.   

As I said, in terms of the increase of gasoline production this year, the industry, I know it surprised a lot of people, but the industry is producing record volumes of gasoline today. But the consumer is burning record volumes of gasoline today, and that's the problem. The consumer has not reacted to these prices yet to alter their habits, the refiners are producing record levels of gasoline volumes.   

If you look at this year versus last year, the industry is producing something over 5.5 million gallons more of gasoline today than they were a year ago.  ExxonMobil's refineries account for half of that increase. So our refineries are operating at very high levels of motor fuels production. So, why don't we build another refinery?   

First, siting and permitting a site is very difficult in this country, as I'm sure all of you can appreciate that; just finding a place where a community will welcome a refinery to be built. The permitting process is very lengthy in its requirements, and it's very costly. There's a lot of discussion in Washington about ways to streamline that process so that it doesn't take so long, it doesn't cost so much to make your way through the permitting process. Whether that comes about or not remains to be seen.   

Thirdly though, we now have an international energy policy that focuses on biofuels. Something many of you are very interested and concerned with. Setting these mandates for biofuels volumes and mandates for biofuel content in gasoline. But if we do the numbers, you don't need another refinery, if these biofuel objectives are to be met and they're mandated to be met.   

So taking the risk to build a new refinery in the face of this kind of an environment would be a very risky proposition for most investors. To build a grassroots refinery. So that's why instead, what we're going to continue to see is refineries everywhere will continue to grow the capacity of their existing sites.   

Because that's the lower risk, lower cost way to continue to grow the volume of gasoline that the US refining infrastructure can produce. And I think you'll find that's going to be the case fairly broadly for a very fundamental reason. Just economics and the risk of uncertainty about the future, particularly given the country's policy around transportation fuels and the uncertainty around how that's going to play out. So that's the refinery question.   

Let's see, let me try to make sure I go to somebody who's not had the opportunity to speak. Yes, sir?

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: DAVID MARTNO
speaker: Investor
text:
Mr. Chairman, Board of Directors. My name is [David Martno] and on behalf of the shareholders I'm going to speak at a little different angle. 50 years ago, when I was in college, I had a job with a company called Humble Oil and Refining. They gave me a roustabout job. It helped put me through college. [And] roustabout at that time, in (inaudible) outside of Corpus Christi, we did.   

We went around and did nothing but clean up any spill, any pipeline leak, all we did. Nobody even knew how to spell EPA back in those days, but they were leading the way at that time. And I look at what you all are doing and listening to the education programs and the magnitude of the studies that you are doing for the global warming and everything and it's not going to be solved.   

But I would like to recommend to all these people that have been complaining about the way you all run your business that they sell their shares, and go ahead and buy Shell, buy BP, whoever it is. Go to their annual meeting, and then you can sit there and complain to them, why can't you all be as performing as Exxon? Thank you.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text: The gentleman down front here.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: ROB BERRIDGE
affiliation: REPRESENTATIVE, INVESTOR NETWORK ON CLIMATE RISK
speaker: Investor
text:
Good morning. My name is Rob Berridge. I'm a member of the staff of the Investor Network on Climate Risk, a network of more than 50 institutional investors with an over 4 trillion in assets under management and the network includes the Connecticut State Treasurer and the California State Controller who have spoken here today.   

I'd like to add -- to respond to that gentleman that many of our investors are long-term investors and they're invested in indexes, and they basically own the whole economy. They're universal investors. And so they don't really see this as a choice of should we sell Exxon or not. It's -- for many of them, it's the largest holding and they would like to see improvement in certain ways that Exxon's doing business.   

So, as Exxon continues to fall behind major competitors in meeting the challenge of delivering low-carbon forms of energy in a carbon constrained world, these investors are concerned about the regulatory and reputational risks that Exxon faces, including the potential for a backlash from law makers, from consumers who might decide not to buy Exxon products, from investors who might decide to divest from Exxon stock, smaller investors, and from job candidates who might decide not to work for Exxon if our company is viewed as part of the global warming problem rather than part of the solution.   

As you know, Exxon has received tens of thousands of letters from consumers, 60,000 letters from members of Co-op America to name just one group in the last few years alone expressing dismay at Exxon's climate policies, the funding of what is perceived to be junk science and the like. So my question is what is Exxon's plan to prevent this kind of movement from snowballing and reducing sales, profits and eventually our stock price? Thank you.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
Well first, because this is about the third time it's been said, we don't fund junk science. And why that's been put there to disparage us is beyond me. And the lists that have been put out about the various groups in London and elsewhere have, when you examine those, they're simply false, they're not true. So that's all I can say to that, I don't have a way to respond to it other than it's not true.   

Now, I've talked a lot about what we are doing and what our plans are, and with respect to the regulatory and legal and the legislative environment, we are actively participating in the discussion around various policy options. And we haven't picked a winner yet, so to speak.   

Because again I think there's -- again it's very complex around how it's going to impact the economy and the economic performance of the US economy, as well as the economy of other countries once policies are put in place, and that's very important to the performance of  ExxonMobil shares in the future as well.   

If the economy's doing well, we typically do well. If the economy's not doing so well, we don't do so well either. So we're very concerned about the policy decisions being selected, that there will be a very good, thorough discussion around the impacts of those and the mechanics of how they would work, and that they not set up winners and losers in the economy.   

The second is, that those policies really need to be adaptable to future changes and conditions. And this is again grounded in our view of this issue. There's a lot of things we understand, there's a lot of things we don't. And as we go forward, we're going to continue to make scientific discoveries around this issue. We ought to have policies that can accommodate what we learn. If the situation gets worse, we need to accommodate that. If it gets -- turns out not to be as bad as we thought, we need to accommodate that.   

And then, there's a lot of uncertainty around what the final economic impact will be as we move down the road with these kinds of policies, and if it's more harmful to the economy than we expected, [we'd be] able to adjust to that. If it's not as harmful and we can crank it down a little tighter, that's fine.   

So the policies need to be -- have some flexibility around how they're structured to accommodate the fact that this is an issue that for the next ten, 20, 30 years we're going to continue to learn things about. Finally at some point, you have to attack this globally. So whatever policies we're putting in place, we hope can set a stage for a global approach and solution.   

Now relative to the threats to  ExxonMobil, within this context and this regulatory environment, we're dealing with it now. We have significant holdings in Europe, where the Kyoto Protocols have been in place now for some time. We developed,  ExxonMobil developed, the greenhouse gas protocol that's used in the Netherlands. It was adopted by the government, and it's now put forth as a best practice on how to measure and account for your greenhouse gas emissions. So we are actively engaged in how to address this issue from a policy standpoint.   

Within Europe, our operations have performed well under those constraints. They're going to get tighter. So it's going to present us with more challenges. But it presents all of our competitors with challenges too. And the steps and the actions we're taking, we're confident, have us well positioned to continue to compete well, taking into consideration what we see others are doing, to see if there's something we can learn from that.   

And again, protect your value for the next ten, 20, 30, 40 years in what we know will continue to be an evolving situation. There isn't going to be a single fix put in place today that's going last forever. So, we've got to be positioned such that we can adapt to whatever that requirement is.   

Others -- and again, I want to try to go to people who have not spoken. The lady in the center there, on the -- I don't think you -- have you spoken? Oh, you have. Yes? Right there. Go ahead.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: RUTH WONG
speaker: Investor
text:
My name is [Ruth Wong]. I attended the shareholders meeting last year and I'm back this year. In the year 2006,  ExxonMobil has invested $733 million in R&D. That sounds like a large number, but for the size of  ExxonMobil and compared to the sales revenue that  ExxonMobil has generated last year, it's only -- it represents -- the R&D expenses represents only [0.2%] of the sales revenue. And I have done research in 12 companies, and  ExxonMobil was ranked the lowest in your R&D efforts.   

Needless to say, R&D is very important. There was a company called Simple Technology. They didn't have a well supported R&D department and the company ran aground in 15 years. The company fell 7 -- by 75% in value.  ExxonMobil might be doing very well at the present time, but in the long run, there might be unforeseen events that might alter the route.   

My second thought is about the dividend strategy. Right now you are paying the shareholders $0.35 per share of the common stock. That comes out to be 1.7% of the current stock valued at approximately $83 per share. And the low dividend in turn raises the risk of the investment in the stock.   

I would like to respond to Denise Nappier's remark about Dr. Boskin's efforts in responding to her questions. And I feel that Dr. Boskin has done a great job in responding in five detailed letters. That's it.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
Thank you. Now with respect to our levels of R&D spend, one of the things that -- the principles that we've always approached is consistency in research -- support for research and development. If you're a researcher, I'm sure you understand one of the most devastating things you can do to a research program is to pull the funding back and forth and back and forth.   

So  ExxonMobil has had a very consistent level of research spending, whether we've had $70 oil prices or $10 oil prices. We've maintained a very high level of support for our research activities. And it's been in that $600 million to $700 million range, the good times, the bad times, because you just can't take those programs up and down based on revenues or profits, if you're really going to impact your business over the long term.   

The second point I'd make is our research -- and I mentioned in my remarks, our research spending is well above that of any of our competitors over the last five, ten years. We hold more patents by far than anyone in this business. So, I think we have a very robust technology effort underway, and it's evident in the business results because that's really what's producing these business results, is the strong technology support.   

I'll take one last question, the gentleman in the tan suit right here. Or, comment.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting

speaker: Investor
text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I'm here representing [Robert Ludwig] and I just have a quick question and a comment. I'm a recent graduate from the Geological Science Department here at SMU. And -- .

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text: Congratulations.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: UNIDENTIFIED AUDIENCE MEMBER
speaker: Investor
text:
Thank you.   

And I'd like to make a brief comment in support of the renewable energy proposal, number 17, in light of the perspective I have in terms of attending SMU. They're leading researchers in geothermal energy, using oil and gas -- what's pumped from oil and fills throughout Texas and the Gulf States.   

And perhaps that would be a starting point maybe for entering the renewable energy market from all the existing oil and gas wells,  ExxonMobil, all the assets it has since there are so many in the Gulf State region that produce oil and water mixtures that can produce electricity at the right temperatures. The formations they're pumped from are very favorable temperatures for generation of electricity.   

And recently well because renewable energy credit demand is skyrocketing, every year Rupert Murdoch's  News Corporation just announced that it would be reducing their greenhouse -- making a goal for greenhouse gas reduction of like 10% in a few years, but the remaining amount that they would offset with -- and there's no other way to offset it, but to buy renewable energy credits.   

So given that guaranteed demand, perhaps a starting point is just as  ExxonMobil invested in the cogen plants across the world, it's the same concept just at the oil well, using the fluids produced to generate electricity, reduce costs, which is an argument that can be used against -- the Board argument against number 17 because of the fact that it doesn't reduce the -- it doesn't divert investment away from more profitable assets.   

And finally to my question, I think you -- your company already donates a considerable amount to SMU Geological Sciences and because of that partnership, are you all willing to investigate geo -- utilizing the geothermal energy potential from oil and gas fields like I believe BP and Shell are looking at too now? Thanks.

title: Exxon Mobil Corporation Shareholders Meeting
name: REX TILLERSON
speaker: Exxon
text:
We have investigated geothermal as an option in the past. We're relooking at it again. One of the principles that we typically take in all these new technologies is that we're very cautious and reluctant to invest in technologies that are dependent upon tax credits or subsidies to make them viable. And that's because those tax subsidies and credits can be as easily pulled away as they can be put in place.   

And secondly, as we're already seeing, if an oil company like  ExxonMobil pursues a renewable fuels option that has a tax credit or mandate, the response of Washington is well, we need to take that away from them because they don't need it. So the economics of those investments are -- become very difficult.   

Having said that though, that really is where we're following all the renewable space. We monitor all of the technology developments that are underway across the entire spectrum of renewables, including geothermal. We have supported some programs at other universities around geothermal options from a research standpoint because I think that is where we're -- we need to make some more progress in the technology so that it can stand on its own economic viability without a lot of government tax support. But thank you for your question.
